governanceNotes: Authored conservatively as ASSOCIATION_ONLY: case-series and cohort literature documents pathological fracture through cyst-weakened bone and growth disturbance adjacent to an active physis in untreated benign bone cysts, but the evidence base is small case series (n=3 to n=4) with multiple competing mechanisms for the growth-arrest outcome (physeal penetration, fracture involvement of the physis, cortisone injection, increased cyst pressure), so individual attribution requires orthopedic review rather than this mapping, and the mapping asserts co-occurrence within the cyst population only.

The catalog target is malunion / nonunion of fractures, a fracture-outcome identity, not growth arrest itself; the mapping is therefore bounded to the fracture-healing-complication pathway the target identity actually represents.

nexusClaim.associationBasis: The benign-bone-cyst literature documents pathological fracture as the common presenting event of cyst-weakened bone (the proximal-femur and proximal-humerus locations being classic) and, in the same lesion population, reports fracture-related and cyst-related healing complications: a femoral head and neck benign-lesion systematic review found 20.8 percent of patients presenting with pathological fracture and 12.5 percent local recurrence after curettage, and simple-cyst case series document growth arrest after pathological fracture through the physis.
nexusClaim.causationStatus: Neither causation nor aggravation is established at the mapping level for this edge: the cited studies document cyst population co-occurrence rather than controlled estimates of fracture-healing-complication rates attributable to cysts, malunion and nonunion in any individual have competing determinants (fracture location and displacement, immobilization adequacy, patient age and biology) that orthopedic assessment must separate, and the growth-arrest literature explicitly lists iatrogenic and treatment mechanisms among the candidate causes, so the mapping asserts lesion-population co-occurrence only.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: A hypothesized structural-weakening pathway is described in the benign-bone-lesion literature: cyst expansion resorbs and thins the surrounding cancellous and cortical bone, reducing its load-bearing cross-section so that normal or minor trauma produces fracture through the lesion, and the same reduced-bone-stock environment plus the lesion cavity itself can impair stable reduction and consolidation, predisposing the fracture to malunion or nonunion; the case-series growth-arrest reports additionally document physeal involvement when the cyst abuts an open growth plate. This physiology explains co-occurrence within the cyst population, but it does not establish that any individual's fracture-healing complication was caused by the cyst rather than by fracture geometry, fixation adequacy, or biology, so no directional claim is asserted here.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: This relationship is supported as an association only. Pathological fracture and healing complications co-occur in the benign-bone-cyst population, but individual determination requires imaging documentation of the cyst and fracture with chronology, orthopedic assessment of healing outcome (malunion or nonunion against accepted radiographic criteria), and exclusion of competing mechanical and biological determinants, all reviewed case by case by a qualified medical professional.
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: Imaging documentation of the bone cyst with location, size, and relationship to the physis or cortical bone; documentation of the pathological or subsequent fracture with date; radiographic healing assessment establishing malunion or nonunion against accepted criteria; treatment records (immobilization, curettage, grafting, fixation) separating lesion-related from treatment-related determinants; a medical professional's opinion connecting the documented findings in this individual case
alternativeEtiologiesToRuleOut: Fracture geometry, displacement, or inadequate immobilization as the primary determinant of the healing complication
Surgical or corticosteroid treatment of the cyst (iatrogenic physeal or osseous injury) rather than the cyst itself
Underlying metabolic bone disease or osteoporosis impairing consolidation independently
Infection or other secondary complication of fracture or surgery driving nonunion

suggestions.rationale: Authored conservatively at association-only strength: the fracture and healing-complication co-occurrence in the benign-bone-cyst population is documented, but the evidence base is small series and the individual determinants of malunion and nonunion are multifactorial, so this edge flags the lesion-population association for evidence-gap review only and must never be presented as established causation or aggravation.
evidenceGaps: Imaging-documented bone cyst with location and chronology
Documented fracture with radiographic healing outcome
Orthopedic assessment separating lesion-related from treatment-related and biological determinants
A medical professional's opinion connecting the documented findings in this individual case

sourceReferences.citation: Clayer M, Boatright C, Conrad E. Growth disturbances associated with untreated benign bone cysts. Aust N Z J Surg. 1997;67(12):872-873. PMID 9451345. doi:10.1111/j.1445-2197.1997.tb07616.x.
sourceReferences.note: Case series of three patients documenting growth disturbance from benign bone cysts adjacent to an active physis in the absence of surgical intervention, with physeal penetration, pathological fracture, and curettage listed as candidate mechanisms; supports the lesion-population co-occurrence proposition and the competing-mechanism caution, not individual causation.

sourceReferences.citation: Shi J, Zhao Z, Yan T, Guo W, Yang R, Tang X, Qu H, Dong S. Surgical treatment of benign osteolytic lesions in the femoral head and neck: a systematic review. BMC Musculoskelet Disord. 2021;22(1):549. PMID 34134687. doi:10.1186/s12891-021-04442-y.
sourceReferences.note: Systematic review of 33 articles (274 patients) reporting 20.8 percent pathological-fracture presentation among benign osteolytic lesions with documented recurrence and joint-preservation outcomes after curettage; supports the fracture co-occurrence proposition in the lesion population, not a fracture-healing-complication causal estimate.
